findings.matters: EFS councils face increased central scrutiny, and the funding route (capitalising revenue spend and repaying through disposals or borrowing) is one a finance director elsewhere may be considering.

findings.headline: Fraudulent tenancies recovered were 29 in Q2 against a target of 40, with a 22% reduction on the same period last year

findings.matters: Recovering properties from tenancy fraud is a counter-fraud outcome that a finance director would compare with their own recovery figures and the court delays affecting them.

findings.headline: Substance misuse grants from central government have been incorporated into core funding from 2026-27, with 2,116 adults in treatment in August 2026
findings.detail: The paper says the previously grant-funded services now sit within core funding and will continue to support employment and housing needs alongside treatment.
findings.matters: A shift from grant to core funding changes the council's budget baseline, which a finance director or a peer council facing the same grant change would want to see.
findings.figures: 2,116 adults in substance misuse treatment (August 2026); grants incorporated into core funding from 2026-27
findings.quote: This drive in numbers has been supported by additional grants from central government, which have now been incorporated into core funding from 2026-27

findings.detail: The paper says the target is the average number of homes that need consent each quarter to meet London Plan requirements. It lists three schemes resolved for approval on 22 September 2026 that are awaiting S106 agreements.
findings.matters: Consent volumes feed the council's future housing and capital pipeline, and a finance director would compare the pipeline of resolved schemes with their own consent position.

findings.headline: The proportion of homes not meeting the Decent Homes Standard was 15.2% in Q2 against an 11% target, down from 16.2%
findings.detail: The paper says a systems and data cleansing exercise at the start of the financial year changed the reporting position with the social housing regulator on non-decency. It says the investment programme addressing the causes will complete in April 2028.
findings.matters: A reporting-basis change agreed with the regulator, and a multi-year investment programme, are both points a finance director or lender would want to track against the council's capital plan.
findings.figures: 15.2% of homes not meeting the Decent Homes Standard; target of 11%; down from 16.2%; programme completing April 2028

findings.headline: Average days to process changes in circumstances in Housing Benefit and Council Tax Support were 20.77 days in September 2026 against a 17-day target
findings.detail: The paper attributes the miss to high volumes of DWP-notified changes and problems with Robotic Process Automation. It says processing times are 150% longer than in September 2025 and that benefits are not expected to improve until Q4.
findings.matters: Slower processing of benefit changes is linked in the paper to both underpayments and overpayments, which matter to finance teams managing benefit subsidy and recovery.
findings.figures: 20.77 days; target of 17 days; processing times 150% longer than September 2025
findings.quote: Issues with Robotic Process Automation have impacted our ability to process DWP generated Change In Circumstances as quickly as we would like which has led to the target being missed.

findings.headline: Successful homelessness prevention outcomes were 73% in Q2 against a 75% target
findings.detail: The paper says this is slightly short of target but well above London-wide and national averages. It does not give those comparator figures.
findings.matters: Prevention outcomes affect how many households reach temporary accommodation, so a finance officer tracking homelessness costs would compare this with their own prevention rate.
findings.figures: 73% successful homelessness prevention outcomes in Q2; target of 75%
findings.quote: The proportion of successful homelessness prevention outcomes in Q2 was 73%.

findings.headline: Lambeth moved 586 households out of temporary accommodation in the year to date against a target of 525
findings.detail: The paper says this is ahead of target and attributes the progress to offering long-term temporary accommodation residents a move into social housing. Homelessness prevention is also a stated focus.
findings.matters: Moves into social housing are a route for reducing temporary accommodation placements, which a finance director at this or another council would compare with their own move-on performance.
findings.figures: 586 households moved out of TA in the year to date; target of 525
findings.quote: At Quarter 2 we had moved 586 households out of TA in the year to date, comfortably ahead of our target of 525.

findings.headline: Lambeth had 4,150 households in temporary accommodation at Quarter 2, including 5,570 children, a 13% reduction since the early 2025 peak
findings.detail: The paper says council efforts are reducing temporary accommodation numbers and gives the reduction since the peak. It also describes the challenge as remaining very large.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation numbers are a demand line that finance officers at this council and peers can compare against their own household counts and placement trends.
findings.figures: 4,150 households in TA; 5,570 children; 13% reduction since the peak reported in early 2025
findings.quote: As of Quarter 2 there were 4,150 households in TA across the borough, including 5,570 children.

findings.headline: 78% of targeted indicators were achieving target in Q2 2026/27, with 31 indicators significantly improved and 16 significantly worsened
findings.detail: The paper reports that 10% more of targeted indicators were within 5% of target. It records 31 indicators with significant improvement against 16 with significant decline in Q2.
findings.matters: A finance director comparing council performance reporting would note the overall balance of improvement and decline across the framework, which is the paper's headline measure of delivery.
findings.figures: 78% of targeted indicators; further 10% within 5% of target; 31 indicators significantly improved; 16 indicators significantly worsened
findings.quote: Most recently reported data shows that 78% of targeted indicators are achieving their target, with a further 10% performing within 5% of target.

findings.headline: Of 14 savings proposals with equalities analyses, 3 are assessed as having an overall negative impact on groups with protected characteristics, 10 neutral and 1 positive.
findings.detail: The Equalities and Justice Panel considered these on 3 November. The three negative assessments relate to Integrated Health and Adult Social Care proposals based on fee and charge increases, which the paper says are benchmarked against other boroughs.
findings.matters: Equalities assessments on savings proposals are a required step other councils will need to complete before their own budget decisions.
findings.figures: 14 proposals totalling £2.906M; 3 negative; 10 neutral; 1 positive
findings.quote: 3 proposals were assessed to have an overall negative impact on groups with protected characteristics, 10 neutral and 1 positive.

findings.headline: The capital investment programme is under review to minimise future borrowing and associated revenue costs.
findings.detail: Cabinet is asked to note the latest position on this review. No borrowing totals are given in the extract.
findings.matters: A council reviewing its capital programme to reduce borrowing is a signal lenders and peers will want to track against their own borrowing plans.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this extract
findings.quote: the latest position on the review of the Capital Investment Programme to minimise future borrowing and associated revenue costs.

findings.headline: Transitional funding protection is expected to end in 2029/30.
findings.detail: The paper says the greater pressures forecast for future years are particularly linked to this end date.
findings.matters: The end of transitional protection is a known cliff edge for the MTFS, and other councils with similar protections will face the same timing question.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this extract
findings.quote: particularly when transitional funding protection is expected to end in 2029/30.

findings.headline: Lambeth presents a management action plan responding to an independent review of its compliance with the CIPFA Financial Management Code.
findings.detail: The review was considered by the Audit and Risk Committee on 22 October 2026. The action plan (Appendix E) will be monitored at regular intervals by that committee.
findings.matters: Finance directors elsewhere can compare the review's recommendations and how they are being addressed against their own FM Code assessments.
findings.figures: Review considered by Audit and Risk Committee on 22 October 2026
findings.quote: the report presents the management action plan to address the recommendations made by the review.

findings.headline: The asset disposals programme is aimed at repaying Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.detail: The paper reports on the forecast capital spend for the year and an update on the disposals programme. A Part II appendix with the disposal pipeline is exempt from disclosure.
findings.matters: Repaying EFS through disposals ties Lambeth's capital receipts directly to its exceptional financial support position, which lenders and other councils in the same position will be watching.
findings.figures: No figure given in this extract
findings.quote: provides an update on the asset disposals programme aimed at repaying Exceptional Financial Support (EFS)

findings.headline: Lambeth plans £5.170m of flexible use of capital receipts to fund development and implementation of budget proposals.
findings.detail: Cabinet is asked to note this use of capital receipts. The paper's recommendations separately cover disposals for repaying Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts for revenue budget proposals is a flexibility other councils also rely on, and the amount is a benchmark for comparison.
findings.figures: £5.170m flexible use of capital receipts
findings.quote: to support the development and implementation of budget proposals up to a value of £5.170m.

findings.headline: Resources overspend is attributed to Finance, where staffing savings are delayed.
findings.detail: The paper says the main overspend within Resources sits in Finance and relates to delays in delivering staffing savings. Temporary Accommodation's overspend is linked to a similar delay in progressing new saving proposals, which the paper expects to be fully achieved in 2027-28.
findings.matters: Staffing savings delivered late are a recurring source of in-year overspend that finance teams elsewhere will be tracking.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this extract
findings.quote: The main overspend within Resources is attributed to Finance with the overspend related to delays in delivering staffing savings.

findings.detail: The savings are split by directorate: Integrated Health and Adult Social Care £2,310k, Growth and Environment £150k and Resources £766k over the three years. The paper says they contribute to closing the estimated gap.
findings.matters: Peers and lenders can measure this first tranche against the £19.096m 2027-28 gap to judge how much of the gap it addresses.

findings.quote: Proposed savings totalling £3.226m are included in Appendix 1

findings.headline: Lambeth must close a £19.096m gap to set a balanced 2027-28 budget, against a July MTFS gap of £93.217m over three years to 2029-30.
findings.detail: The paper says the first tranche of savings is intended to start closing the gap over the MTFS period. The £19.096m figure is the gap for 2027-28 specifically.
findings.matters: The size of the 2027-28 gap relative to the three-year gap shows how much of the budget problem is front-loaded, which affects lender and peer expectations.
findings.figures: £19.096m gap for 2027-28; £93.217m three-year gap to 2029-30 as presented in July
findings.quote: To set a balanced budget for 2027 -28, the Council will need to close a gap of £19.096m.

findings.headline: Growth and Environment moves adversely by £6.442m, while the other directorates move favourably.

Corporate Items also moved favourably, mainly from reducing the corporate hold for Growth and Environment mitigations and a review of year-end accruals.
findings.matters: Income-target shortfalls combined with delayed savings are a pattern other councils' services may recognise in their own monitoring.

findings.quote: With an adverse movement in Growth and Environment of £6.442m, offset by favourable movements across all the other directorates.

findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the size and direction of this in-year movement with their own Q2 position.

findings.headline: Savills has been appointed to validate the assumptions behind the 30-year HRA Business Plan, to ensure it remains balanced
findings.detail: The report says Savills were appointed to validate the council's assumptions so the HRA Business Plan remains balanced in the short, medium and long term. The revised plan goes to Cabinet in January 2027, with scrutiny in advance.
findings.matters: An external review of the business plan's assumptions, carried out before the 2027/28 budget and rent decisions, is the independent check a lender or peer finance director would look for.
findings.quote: validate the Council’s assumptions to ensure that the Council’s HRA Business Plan remains balanced in the short, medium, and long term.

findings.headline: Capitalisation of high-value revenue repairs and officer staff costs will now be posted quarterly, not at year end
findings.detail: The report says high-value revenue repairs and staff costs of officers working on capital projects have historically been transferred to capital at year end. This is now being posted each quarter to give better tracking of actual capital spend.
findings.matters: A change in when revenue costs are capitalised affects the reported capital and revenue position through the year, which finance directors at other councils would want to know when comparing in-year figures.
findings.quote: This is now being posted each quarter to provide better tracking of actual capital spend.

findings.headline: Lambeth has spent £21m buying back 62 properties since February 2025
findings.detail: The report says the HRA acquisition programme is funded from Local Authority Housing Funding, Right to Buy receipts and HRA borrowing, and that the properties acquired are mostly ex-Right to Buy homes.
findings.matters: Acquisitions funded partly by HRA borrowing add to the debt that the business plan must support, which a lender or peer council would weigh alongside the EFS repayment.
findings.figures: £21m spent; 62 properties
findings.quote: From February 2025, we have spent £21m buying back 62 properties.

findings.headline: Over £140m of contracts have been procured since April 2026/27 to deliver the five-year Capital Plan
findings.detail: The report says that since April 2026/27 the council has procured over £140m of contracts for the five-year Capital Plan. It states that capital investment will reduce the need for reactive repairs, which is a key assumption in the revised 30-year HRA Business Plan.
findings.matters: Procurement of this scale ahead of delivery is a concrete step that a finance director can measure against the plan, and the reduction in reactive repairs is the efficiency the business plan depends on.
findings.figures: over £140m of contracts procured
findings.quote: have successfully procured over £140m of contracts to enable the delivery

findings.headline: The revised 2026/27 housing capital programme is estimated at £53.9m, against an average of £35 million a year in major works
findings.detail: The report gives a revised 2026/27 housing capital estimate of £53.9m. It says the major works investment has averaged £35 million a year, and that spend is expected to be concentrated in the last two quarters of the year.
findings.matters: A year-end spend concentration of this size is a delivery and forecasting risk that finance directors and lenders watch closely, particularly where the programme is being scaled up.
findings.figures: £53.9m (revised 2026/27 housing capital programme estimate); £35 million a year (average major works investment)
findings.quote: The council’s revised 2026/27 housing capital programme is estimated at £53.9m.

findings.headline: Higher Risk Building capital works have been delayed pending Building Safety Regulator approval
findings.detail: The report says capital investment in Higher Risk Buildings has been delayed while approval is obtained from the Building Safety Regulator. It also says project-by-project procurement slows mobilisation compared with previous Qualifying Long Term Agreement arrangements.
findings.matters: Regulatory approval delays on building safety works push spend and safety outcomes back, and the procurement comparison is directly relevant to other councils choosing between project-by-project procurement and framework or long-term agreements.
findings.quote: Capital investment in assets has been delayed for Higher Risk Buildings due to obtaining Building Safety Regulator (BSR) approval.

findings.headline: The plan assumes operational revenue savings from 2027/28 to meet the additional borrowing costs of the capital programme
findings.detail: The report says operational revenue savings have been assumed from 2027/28 to fund the extra borrowing costs. It also records the risk that anticipated revenue savings fail to materialise, scored 12 on the council's risk matrix, the same score as the business plan not being balanced.
findings.matters: A plan that depends on savings to pay for new borrowing is exposed if the savings do not arrive, which is the scenario a lender would test and a finance director elsewhere would compare against their own savings delivery.
findings.figures: risk score 12 (likelihood 3 x impact 4); savings from 2027/28
findings.quote: From 2027/28 operational revenue savings have been assumed in the plan that will be required to fund the additional borrowing costs

findings.headline: The HRA Business Plan projects capital investment rising over the first five years, funded by borrowing supported by future rent
findings.detail: The summary says the initial projections increase capital investment over the first five years and that the increase will be funded by borrowing. The report notes that investment decisions have wider implications for the long-term business plan and the viability of the HRA.
findings.matters: Growing HRA borrowing against future rent, while the council is also repaying EFS, is a debt-service trajectory a lender or peer council would need to see in the 30-year plan.
findings.figures: first 5 years (projection period)
findings.quote: with the increase investment to be funded by borrowing which is supported by future rent.

findings.headline: Asset disposal income is to be applied to repaying the EFS loan, with £3.318m of residential disposals achieved in 2025/6 and a further pipeline valued above £13M
findings.detail: The report says £3.318m was achieved from residential asset disposals in 2025/6. Garages, land, residential and hostel assets valued in excess of £13M have been recommended for disposal this financial year, with them due to come to market around Q4 2026/7.
findings.matters: The EFS repayment depends on these disposals completing on the stated timetable, so a finance director or lender can test the repayment plan against the pipeline value and the Q4 timing.
findings.figures: £3.318m residential disposals (2025/6); valued in excess of £13M (pipeline); c.Q4 2026/7 (timing)
findings.quote: Assets including garages, land, residential and hostels have been identified and recommended for disposal this financial year, these assets are valued in excess of £13M and would come to market c.Q4 2026/7.

findings.headline: Lambeth received £40m of Exceptional Financial Support in 2025/26 as a loan it must repay, with repayment to come from disposals of HRA assets
findings.detail: The report says the £40m was to address the disrepair backlog and is repayable. It identifies disposal of non-operational or beyond-economic-repair HRA assets as the repayment route, and says no further EFS request is currently anticipated for 2026/27.
findings.matters: A council that has taken exceptional support as a repayable loan and is funding repayment from asset sales is carrying a specific repayment obligation that a lender or peer finance officer would want to track against delivery of the disposals.
findings.quote: In 2025/26, it received £40m of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) to address its disrepair backlog. This funding is a loan and therefore repayable.

findings.headline: Lift replacement, budgeted at £950,000, is listed as awaiting Building Safety Regulator approval, with works anticipated early 2027.
findings.detail: The lift replacement is recorded as 'Awaiting BSR approval' with works anticipated early 2027. Several other schemes, including the roof project and external wall insulation, are shown as going through Building Safety Regulator (BSR) application stages before works start.
findings.matters: Regulator sign-off that gates the start of works is a delivery dependency that finance officers at other councils with higher-risk building stock also have to schedule spend around.

findings.quote: Lift replacement Awaiting BSR

findings.headline: SME invoices paid within 10 days stand at 71% against an 80% target, up from 64% in Quarter 1
findings.detail: Overall invoices paid within 30 days are at 96%, meeting the target, with September at 97%. The paper attributes the 30-day performance to improved staffing levels, training and technical partner collaboration.
findings.matters: Late payment to SMEs is a supplier-market and procurement risk that other councils will track alongside their own payment-performance targets.
findings.figures: 71% SME invoices paid within 10 days; 80% target; 64% in Quarter 1; 96% invoices paid within 30 days; 60,799 total invoices
findings.quote: SME performance for Q2 stands at 71%, an improvement on the 64% achieved in Quarter

findings.headline: The HRA forecasts a £2.510m surplus, which includes £18m of the £27m disrepair provision
findings.detail: The HRA surplus is mainly from reduced interest on borrowing and reduced void loss, with an overspend on repairs from clearing the voids backlog. The paper says the disrepair provision is intended to cover ongoing costs of resolving historic claims.
findings.matters: A HRA surplus that depends on drawing only part of a large disrepair provision is a risk other housing finance teams will want to understand when judging their own exposure to historic claims.

findings.quote: The forecast includes £18m of the £27m provision for Housing Disrepair costs

findings.headline: The MTFS gap is £19.096m for 2027-28 and £93.217m to 2029-30, and first budget proposals are brought forward to close it

findings.matters: A council with a multi-year gap of this size, with the first savings tranche now in front of members, is one other councils and lenders will compare against their own medium-term savings plans.
findings.quote: The July update of the Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) saw the gap for 2027-28 reduced to £19.096m and to £93.217m up to 2029-30.

findings.headline: General Fund balance is around the S151 officer's recommended 10% of net revenue expenditure, while earmarked reserves 'remain low'

findings.matters: The gap between a General Fund balance at the recommended level and thin earmarked reserves is the position finance directors need to assess when judging a council's capacity to absorb further in-year pressures.

findings.quote: General Fund Balance is now around the level recommended by the S151 officer (10% of net revenue expenditure)

findings.headline: Total external debt stood at £1.118bn at 30 September 2026, a decrease of £9.2m in the quarter

findings.matters: A lender or finance director tracking a council's debt trajectory will want the quarterly movement and the mix between PWLB and local authority borrowing.

findings.quote: Total external debt outstanding at 30 September 2026 was £1.118bn, a decrease of £9.2m in the quarter.

findings.headline: Asset disposals are the planned means of funding the EFS, with a disposal pipeline to be progressed through formal decisions
findings.detail: The paper says EFS will be funded by capitalising day-to-day spend, with the cost of borrowing and MRP if funded that way. A disposal pipeline is listed in Appendix C and will go through formal decision-making. The paper also notes a CIL approval request.
findings.matters: Relying on a disposal programme to fund capitalised revenue spend is a route other EFS councils will be watching for both its delivery and its effect on borrowing costs.

findings.quote: The Capital budget for 2026-27 is forecasting an underspend of £19.873m

findings.detail: The paper notes that a second year of the High Needs Stability Grant may be confirmed for 2027-28, and that an application could offset part of the deficit. The council's net surplus across DSG blocks at 31 March 2026 was £2.195m, and it did not qualify on that basis.
findings.matters: Eligibility for the DfE stability grant turns on the DSG position at a set date, so other councils near that threshold will want to see how the test was applied to Lambeth.

findings.quote: Lambeth did not, however, qualify in 2026/27 for the 2025/26 High Needs Stability Grant

findings.detail: The DSG in-year overspend is forecast at £20.433m against funding, with the High Needs Block driving most of the increase. The council says it will rely on the DSG statutory override. It did not qualify for the 2025/26 High Needs Stability Grant.
findings.matters: A forecast swing from a DSG surplus to a deficit of this size, with no confirmed grant relief, is a high-needs pressure other councils and lenders will want to track.

findings.quote: This forecast would leave a net DSG deficit position at 31st March 2027 of £18.238m

findings.headline: Housing Services (GF) forecasts a £5.305m overspend because additional 2026-27 savings are not being achieved in the timeframe planned
findings.detail: The paper reports £1.3m of savings achieved, offset by the cost of staff taken on to deliver the savings package. It expects the full-year impact to come through in 2027-28. Temporary accommodation nightly-paid costs are shown as a £7.000m pressure, partly offset by incentive savings.
findings.matters: A savings business case slipping a year, with the cost of delivery staff sitting in the forecast, is a pattern finance directors managing temporary accommodation pressures will recognise.

findings.headline: Corporate Items forecasts a £15.960m underspend, which the paper says offsets £5.125m of undelivered prior-year and cross-cutting savings
findings.detail: The underspend is mainly from corporately held risk contingencies (£14.1m), including £11.0m of saving and growth contingency, and a £4.524m debt and financing underspend. The paper states these items offset the £5.125m pressure from undelivered savings.
findings.matters: Balancing undelivered savings with one-off contingency and debt-financing underspends is a position other councils with savings gaps will want to compare against their own contingency headroom.
findings.figures: £15.960m Corporate Items underspend; £14.1m corporate risk budgets; £11.0m saving and growth contingency; £4.524m debt and financing underspend; £5.125m undelivered savings pressure
findings.quote: Overall, Corporate Items are forecasting to underspend by £15.960m, a favourable movement of £3.359m from quarter 1.

findings.headline: Growth and Environment forecasts a £15.045m adverse variance, a deterioration of £6.442m since Quarter 1
findings.detail: The paper attributes the worsening mainly to delayed delivery of planned mitigations and lower-than-expected income, particularly in Parking. Further mitigations are being identified for Quarter 3.
findings.matters: A large income-target shortfall in parking and regulatory services, with mitigations still unidentified, is a pressure other councils with similar fee and charges savings will recognise.
findings.figures: £15.045m adverse variance; £6.442m deterioration from Quarter 1; £3.161m Parking Services pressure; £1.327m Community Safety savings at risk
findings.quote: Growth & Environment is forecasting an adverse variance of £15.045m at Period 6, representing a deterioration of £6.442m since Quarter 1.

findings.headline: Exceptional Financial Support of £116m across 2024-25 to 2026-27 was approved in principle by MHCLG in February 2026
findings.detail: The EFS is described as allowing the council to increase reserves and provisions at the end of 2024-25, meet the 2025-26 overspend and balance the 2026-27 budget. It is to be repaid through a planned programme of asset disposals, and MHCLG will increase scrutiny of progress.
findings.matters: An EFS council's financing route, the capitalisation cost and the reliance on asset sales are the facts other councils and lenders need to judge whether the support is a bridge or a structural fix.
findings.figures: £116m EFS, 2024-25 to 2026-27 in declining amounts
findings.quote: the Council’s application for £116m of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) was approved in principle by MHCLG

findings.headline: Lambeth's General Fund forecast overspend is £8.592m at Quarter 2, £0.711m better than Quarter 1
findings.detail: The report states the General Fund overspend has improved from Quarter 1. Service area overspends rose by £2.656m, offset by a favourable movement in Corporate Items. Growth and Environment's adverse movement is the largest single driver of the service-area increase.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the size and direction of a second-year EFS council's in-year overspend against its own forecast, and see how corporate contingencies are being used to offset service pressures.

findings.quote: At quarter two, the General Fund forecast overspend is £8.592m, an improvement of £0.711m from the quarter one position.

findings.matters: Income projections that have not been tested against timing can move a council's in-year position, which is a question a finance director at another council would want answered.

findings.matters: Staff savings are often the largest and most timing-sensitive part of a savings programme, so whether they are reprofiled in the forecast matters to peers and to lenders.

findings.detail: The request covers both HRA and General Fund disposals, and the Committee wants the report before any Cabinet decision. Officers say asset disposal information will be included in the Quarter 2 report.
findings.matters: Exceptional Financial Support is a government-approved funding route, and a council repaying it through asset sales is a position that finance directors and lenders track closely.

findings.detail: The Committee asked whether savings already in the 2026/27 forecast had been rigorously reviewed, so that 'baked in savings' were not simply carried forward into later years. The officer response is that the review is under way and will feed the updated MTFS.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council, or a lender, would want to know whether a council's previously agreed savings are being tested for deliverability before the next budget is set.

findings.headline: Equalities analysis of 14 savings proposals (£2.906m) finds 3 with overall negative impact, 10 neutral, 1 positive
findings.detail: The Equalities and Justice Panel considered analyses of 14 savings proposals totalling £2.906m for 2027-28 to 2029-30. Three were assessed as having an overall negative impact, concentrated in fee and charge increases within Integrated Health and Adult Social Care, with officers saying the increases are benchmarked against other boroughs.
findings.matters: Equalities impact findings on fee-based savings are a constraint that peer councils considering similar fee increases will want to see assessed.
findings.figures: 14 savings proposals totalling £2.906M; 3 negative, 10 neutral, 1 positive
findings.quote: 3 proposals were assessed to have an overall negative impact on groups with protected characteristics, 10 neutral and 1 positive.

findings.headline: Council forecasts a year-end position to be reported at Quarter 3 with the aim of reducing forecast to within budget by year-end
findings.detail: Recommendation 3 asks members to consider management actions being taken by Corporate Directors to reduce the forecast position to within budget by the end of the financial year. Recommendation 12 confirms the year-end forecast will be reported to February Cabinet after Quarter 3.
findings.matters: A stated aim to bring an £8.592m forecast overspend back within budget by year-end is a specific recovery target that peers and lenders can track through the Quarter 3 report.
findings.figures: £8.592m forecast overspend at end of September 2026
findings.quote: To consider the management actions already being taken by Corporate Directors to reduce the forecast position to within budget by the end of the financial year.

findings.headline: Financial Management Code compliance review produces recommendations with a management action plan monitored by Audit and Risk Committee
findings.detail: Following an independent CIPFA FM Code compliance review considered by Audit and Risk Committee on 22 October 2026, the paper presents a management action plan (Appendix E) to address the review's recommendations. Members are asked to note the plan, which the Audit and Risk Committee will monitor at regular intervals.
findings.matters: An external FM Code compliance review with recommendations is a governance finding that finance directors at peer councils will compare against their own FM Code self-assessments.
findings.quote: Following a recent independent review of the Council's compliance with the Chartered Institute of Finance's (CIPFA) Financial Management (FM) Code the report presents the management action plan to address the recommendations made by the review.

findings.headline: Council to note Quarter 2 review of Capital Investment Programme aimed at minimising future borrowing and revenue costs
findings.detail: Recommendation 6 asks members to note the latest position on the review of the Capital Investment Programme, which the council says aims to minimise future borrowing and associated revenue costs.
findings.matters: A deliberate reduction of future borrowing to limit revenue costs is a choice lenders and peer finance directors track as a signal of capital affordability.
findings.quote: To note the latest position on the review of the Capital Investment Programme to minimise future borrowing and associated revenue costs.

findings.headline: Council says Exceptional Financial Support repayment depends on an asset disposals programme
findings.detail: The summary says the report gives an update on the asset disposals programme aimed at repaying Exceptional Financial Support (EFS). The recommendations ask members to note an indicative Disposal Pipeline for the General Fund and HRA and a Part II Appendix C pipeline to go through formal decision reports.
findings.matters: EFS repayment through disposals is a specific, dependent funding route that lenders and peer councils with EFS exposure will want to see progressing.
findings.quote: The report sets out the forecast capital spend for the year and provides an update on the asset disposals programme aimed at repaying Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) .

findings.headline: Flexible use of capital receipts to support budget proposals up to £5.170m
findings.detail: Members are asked to note the use of flexible use of capital receipts to support the development and implementation of budget proposals up to a value of £5.170m. The paper also describes an asset disposals programme aimed at repaying Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.matters: Use of capital receipts to fund revenue transformation is a flexibility peers use and lenders scrutinise, and the link to EFS repayment via disposals is a specific funding dependency.
findings.figures: £5.170m flexible use of capital receipts
findings.quote: To note the use of flexible use of capital receipts to support the development and implementation of budget proposals up to a value of £5.170m.

findings.detail: Table 1 sets out tranche one savings by directorate: Integrated Health and Adult Social Care £2.310m total, Growth and Environment £150k, and Resources £766k. Savings are phased £2.826m in 2027-28, £375k in 2028-29 and £25k in 2029-30.
findings.matters: A finance director can compare the directorate split and phasing against the size of the stated gap to see how much of the 2027-28 gap the first tranche covers.

findings.quote: Proposed savings totalling £3.226m are included in Appendix 1 and contribute to closing the estimated budget gap over the MTFS period.

findings.headline: Budget gap of £93.217m over three years to 2029-30 in July MTFS, with £19.096m to close for a balanced 2027-28 budget
findings.detail: The latest MTFS presented to Cabinet in July showed a three-year budget gap to 2029-30. The council says it must close a £19.096m gap to set a balanced 2027-28 budget. The paper sets out the first tranche of savings contributing to that gap.
findings.matters: The scale of the gap to be closed for 2027-28 is a direct measure of the council's dependence on further savings and reserves, which a lender and peer finance directors need to weigh.

findings.quote: The latest MTFS position as presented to Cabinet in July was a budget gap of £93.217m over 3 years to 2029 -30. To set a balanced budget for 2027 -28, the Council will need to close a gap of £19.096m.

findings.headline: Finance overspend attributed to delays in delivering staffing savings
findings.detail: The main overspend within Resources is attributed to Finance, relating to delays in delivering staffing savings. Children, Families and Education's pressure is largely from placements, SEN transport and staffing savings delivery.
findings.matters: Staffing-saving delays in finance and children's services are a recognisable delivery risk that finance directors elsewhere will be tracking in their own savings trackers.
findings.quote: The main overspend within Resources is attributed to Finance with the overspend related to delays in delivering staffing savings.

findings.headline: Growth and Environment overspend driven by income target shortfall and delayed savings, with Temporary Accommodation delay on new savings
findings.detail: The paper attributes the main General Fund overspends to Growth and Environment, Housing (Temporary Accommodation) and Children's Social Care. G&E pressure is mainly an income target shortfall and delays to savings programmes; the TA overspend comes from delay in progressing new saving proposals, which the paper expects to be achieved fully in 2027-28.
findings.matters: Shows a savings-delivery slippage pattern (income shortfall and delayed programmes) that peers planning similar demand-led or income-dependent savings will want to test against their own delivery timelines.
findings.figures: Growth and Environment adverse movement £6.442m
findings.quote: The pressure within Growth and Environment is mainly driven by a shortfall against income targets  and delays to the delivery of some savings programmes.

findings.headline: Lambeth projects a £8.592m overspend at end of September 2026, an improvement of £711k from quarter 1
findings.detail: The paper reports the General Fund forecast as an overspend of £8.592m at end of September 2026, down £711k from Quarter 1. Service area overspend rose by £2.656m, with an adverse movement of £6.442m in Growth and Environment offset by favourable movements elsewhere and a favourable Corporate Items movement.
findings.matters: A finance director at another council can compare the size, direction and drivers of the movement against their own mid-year forecast, and a lender sees the in-year position the council expects to carry into year-end.
findings.figures: £8.592m overspend; £711k improvement from Quarter 1; service area overspend increased by £2.656m; Growth and Environment adverse movement £6.442m
findings.quote: The Council is projecting a £8.592m overspend at the end of September 2026, an improvement of £711k from quarter 1.

findings.headline: The Council's quarter one 2026/27 forecast shows a £9.3m overspend after management mitigations.
findings.detail: The overspend is forecast despite the application of management mitigations, and comes alongside a planned savings level of £46.6m for 2026/27.
findings.matters: A first-quarter overspend in the year after a £35.1m outturn overspend shows whether the savings and mitigations are landing, which other councils with similar savings plans would want to see.

findings.quote: The Council’s quarter one reporting for 2026/27 shows a forecast overspend of £9.3m following the application of mitigations by management.

findings.headline: The Council's Dedicated Schools Grant budget is forecast to move to a £12.3m deficit for 2026/27.
findings.detail: The DSG was in a small surplus of £2.2m. The Council has submitted a plan for high needs to the DfE and may request potential funding, but the paper notes a risk that the Council will need to fund its future deficits.
findings.matters: An unfunded DSG deficit that the council may have to meet from its own resources is a pressure that affects reserves and budgets across English councils with high needs demand.
findings.figures: DSG surplus £2.2m; forecast deficit £12.3m for 2026/27
findings.quote: However, it forecasts a deficit of £12.3m for 2026/27.

findings.matters: Unvalidated sundry debtor and creditor balances in a pension fund are a balance-sheet risk that other funds and their auditors would want to understand.

findings.quote: they were unable to provide an estimated date for completion.

findings.headline: The Council has not yet decided the future of Homes for Lambeth, and the associated significant weakness remains for 2025/26.
findings.detail: The Council is undertaking an options appraisal on its future use of Homes for Lambeth. The weakness, first identified in 2021/22, is carried into 2025/26 in the governance and improving economy criteria.
findings.matters: A council-owned housing company with an unresolved future and an open audit weakness is a live decision that affects housing delivery and any associated financial exposure.
findings.figures: Weakness first identified 2021/22; remains for 2025/26
findings.quote: As at the date of this report, the Council continues to consider its options for the future HfL.

findings.headline: 91% of high priority internal audit actions were implemented within agreed timeframes in 2025/26, against a target of 85%, with none overdue at year end.
findings.detail: The Head of Internal Audit gave a reasonable assurance opinion for 2025/26, up from a limited opinion for 2024/25 when 54% of medium and high priority actions were implemented on time. The auditor has treated the internal control weakness as addressed.
findings.matters: A measured shift from 54% on-time implementation to 91% for high priority actions is a concrete governance change a finance director at another council can benchmark against.

findings.quote: 91% of high priority actions were being implemented within agreed timeframes against a target of 85%.

findings.headline: The auditor has closed the 2022/23 weakness on resilience to future pressures, which relates to general fund and HRA reserves.
findings.detail: The auditor records that the weakness is no longer present during 2025/26, following replenishment of the general fund and HRA unallocated reserves and the creation of a financial risk reserve.
findings.matters: A previously identified significant weakness being lifted is the kind of audit outcome that peers and lenders track as evidence of a council's recovery.

findings.quote: This recommendation has been satisfactorily addressed. The weakness was no longer present during 2025/26.

findings.detail: The paper describes this as the minimum acceptable level identified by the Corporate Director of Resources. The auditor concludes the earlier weakness on financial resilience has been addressed, and a £12m financial risk reserve has also been created.
findings.matters: Restoring general fund reserves to the S151 threshold after a period of depletion is a recovery a finance director at another council would compare against their own reserve position.

findings.quote: In 2025/26, the general fund balance has been restored to 10% of the net annual budget

findings.headline: The Council reports a cumulative budget gap of £93.2m up to 2029/30 and a budget gap of £19.2m for 2027/28, with no plan yet to close the gaps without EFS.
findings.detail: The MTFS reflects no use of EFS from 2027/28, and work on a plan to close the gaps is ongoing. The auditor states the Council does not yet have plans to close the gaps without further EFS.
findings.matters: A stated gap with no closing plan and a planned end to EFS is the situation a lender or peer finance director would need to see when judging future borrowing and reserve needs.

findings.quote: cumulative gaps of £93.2m up to 2029/30

findings.detail: EFS permits capitalisation of expenditure, funded through increased borrowing or capital receipts. A further £10.9m was contributed to earmarked reserves, and the MTFS includes the minimum revenue provision charges that follow from the borrowing.
findings.matters: EFS is borrowing-funded capitalisation, so it adds to the Council's debt and minimum revenue provision costs, which lenders and finance directors need to track.

findings.quote: The Council applied for and received £46m of Exceptional Financial Support in 2025/26.

findings.headline: Budgeted savings of £46.2m for 2025/26 were not met, with £21.3m achieved.
findings.detail: The shortfall is incorporated in the service overspends reported for the year. The Council rolled the undelivered savings forward, and the 2026/27 MTFS savings plan rose to £46.6m.
findings.matters: A savings plan delivering under half its target, with the shortfall rolled forward, is the pattern a finance director at another council would test their own plan against.
findings.figures: Budgeted savings £46.2m; achieved £21.3m; 2026/27 planned savings £46.6m
findings.quote: Budgeted savings of £46.2m were not met (only £21.3m were achieved)

findings.headline: The Council's 2025/26 final outturn overspend was £35.1m, against forecasts of between £15m and £20m reported at quarters 1 to 3.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the gap between forecast and outturn to one-off and corporate adjustments, including increased bad debt provisions for parking and sundry debts and a contingency amount. The Council says the bad debt risk was in its quarterly reports but was not estimated because the Accounts Improvement Plan was in progress.
findings.matters: A movement of roughly £15m–£20m between in-year forecasts and final outturn shows that quarterly monitoring did not capture the year-end position, which is what a peer council's monitoring process would need to test.

findings.quote: the quarter 4 final outturn report, and the financial statements reported an overspend of £35.1m.

findings.headline: The Council published its draft statement of accounts on 23 July 2026, three weeks after the statutory deadline of 30 June.
findings.detail: The Council engaged external support for parts of the accounts preparation under its Accounts Improvement Plan. Delays in the group consolidation prevented publication by the statutory deadline.
findings.matters: Late draft accounts and external support for preparation are a signal other finance teams facing the same closedown pressures will recognise, and they feed directly into the backstop disclaimer.

findings.quote: on the 23rd July 2026, three weeks after the statutory deadline of 30th June.

findings.matters: A finance director at any council or a lender will want to know that the Council's accounts for the period carry no audit assurance, which affects confidence in the reported position.
