This leaves 13 awaiting clarification on whether they can be closed or require regularization. Council has resolved 26 of 39 outstanding contracts since early September, showing tangible progress on control issue.
findings.matters: Demonstrates management action reducing contract status uncertainty; shows progress on identified control gap while 13 contracts remain unresolved.
findings.figures: 13 contracts awaiting clarification, down from 39 in early September
findings.quote: This leaves 13 that are awaiting clarification from the contract manager (on whether they can be closed or are still required and hence need to be regularised) (note, this has reduced from 39 in early September)

findings.paper_title: 261013 A&R Committee Report Oct 26 - Procurement & Compliance v1.1
findings.headline: Contract Standing Orders not updated for Procurement Act 2023 despite February 2025 implementation date
findings.detail: Council's Contract Standing Orders have not been fully updated to reflect requirements of the Procurement Act 2023, which came into force in February 2025. This creates inconsistency between internal corporate rules and current legislation, potentially leading to officer uncertainty and increasing non-compliance risk. Update is being treated as priority in improvement programme.
findings.matters: Compliance gap exposes council to legal risk; finance directors at peer councils face identical legislative change obligations.
findings.figures: Procurement Act 2023 came into force February 2025
findings.quote: the council's Contract Standing Orders (CSOs) have not yet been fully updated to reflect the requirements and terminology of the Procurement Act 2023, despite the new regime coming into force in February 2025

findings.paper_title: 261013 A&R Committee Report Oct 26 - Procurement & Compliance v1.1
findings.headline: Purchase orders exceed contract values by £38.08m across council's £3.76bn contract portfolio
findings.detail: The council's contract register shows purchase orders cumulatively exceeding agreed contract values by £38.08m (approximately 1% of total contract value). Meetings with contract managers are underway to verify accuracy and determine corrective actions. Separate work to identify spend occurring without valid contracts will commence this month.
findings.matters: Represents potential unauthorized overspends against contracts, creating legal and financial control risks relevant to lenders monitoring council's control environment.
findings.figures: £38.08m against total contract value of £3.76bn
findings.quote: In total, the value by which purchase orders are showing as exceeding contract values on the central register is £38.08m (against the £3.76bn total contract value on the register)

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Action Plan going into 202627 - Progress Update Oct 26
findings.headline: Internal audit action implementation rates 57% (high-priority) and 58% (medium-priority) fall well below 85% target; 20% of high-priority actions overdue
findings.detail: Council is not implementing identified internal control improvements at planned pace. Implementation rates have declined since previous reporting period. Of remaining open actions, 20% of high-priority and 42% of medium-priority are overdue. Paper notes delays "may prolong the Council's exposure to known governance, financial and operational control weaknesses."
findings.matters: Shows whether council is actually fixing control gaps identified by audit; slow implementation prolongs exposure to known risks and suggests broader execution challenges.
findings.figures: 57% high-priority implementation; 58% medium-priority implementation; 20% high-priority actions overdue; 42% medium-priority actions overdue
findings.quote: Implementation rates have declined since the previous reporting period and remain below the Council's target of at least 85%. The latest Internal Audit progress update reports implementation rates of 57% for high-priority actions and 58% for medium-priority actions. Of the actions that remain open, 20% of high-priority actions and 42% of medium-priority actions are overdue, based on their original target dates.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Action Plan going into 202627 - Progress Update Oct 26
findings.headline: Disrepair litigation cases now decreasing for first time in 2026-27; high-risk complex notices reduced from over 200 to under 80
findings.detail: Court order breaches on disrepair works had been growing but are now decreasing. Council increased staffing and contractor capacity and implemented end-to-end process review; additional claims have been withdrawn following more robust governance. New arbitration scheme in development.
findings.matters: Identifies a growing financial liability that has now been arrested; shows management action is having measurable effect on a previously deteriorating position.
findings.figures: High-risk complex notices reduced from over 200 at start of 2026-27 to under 80; overall case total now decreasing
findings.quote: The overall case total is now decreasing for the first time in 2026-27, with the total number of cases being closed being greater than the number of new cases. The number of high-risk, complex notices has reduced from over 200 at the start of the financial year, to under 80.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Action Plan going into 202627 - Progress Update Oct 26
findings.headline: 2024-25 accounts received backstop disclaimer opinion; 2025-26 accounts due 31 January 2027
findings.detail: 2024-25 accounts were given a disclaimer opinion (auditor unable to form full audit opinion) ahead of national backstop date. Council has commissioned additional QA work, external reviews, and external balance sheet review. Paper states accounts issue "will remain a significant issue until the Council is in a position of receiving an unqualified external audit opinion."
findings.matters: A disclaimer opinion means audited accounts cannot be relied upon; lenders cannot assess true financial position from audited statements.
findings.figures: Backstop disclaimer for 2024-25; deadline for 2025-26 accounts 31 January 2027
findings.quote: The external auditor provided a 'disclaimed' backstop opinion on the Accounts for 2024-25 ahead of the national backstop date on 27 February 2026.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Action Plan going into 202627 - Progress Update Oct 26
findings.headline: Statutory recommendations from external auditors issued February 2025 remain outstanding 19 months later with work to March 2027
findings.detail: External auditors issued statutory recommendations 19 months ago; council reports substantial progress but paper emphasizes ongoing reliance on EFS and that "considerable work to be done to ensure the Council is in a financially sustainable position on an ongoing basis." Deadline for completion is 31 March 2027.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations indicate significant governance and control failures; the duration of the remediation period and continued financial reliance show deep structural issues.
findings.figures: 19 months since February 2025; completion deadline 31 March 2027
findings.quote: The statutory recommendations were issued 19 months ago, and the Council has made substantial progress in addressing both immediate and long-term financial challenges.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Action Plan going into 202627 - Progress Update Oct 26
findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation hotel spending fell from £125,000 to £5,000 per month following December 2025 policy change
findings.detail: New placement policy (December 2025) and out-of-hours process changes delivered dramatic spending reduction. TA case numbers fell from 4767 (February 2025) to 4159 (August 2026). New procurement strategy from April 2026 shifts from expensive nightly-paid accommodation to leased stock, with targets for £1.5m savings and £300k income increase.
findings.matters: TA is a major cost pressure across local government; this shows a specific strategy that has delivered measurable results and is of interest to councils facing same pressures.
findings.figures: Hotel spend dropped from £125,000 to c£5,000 per month; TA numbers from 4,767 to 4,159; targets £1.5m savings and £300k income increase
findings.quote: Hotel expenditure has dropped from £125,000 per month to c£5,000.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Action Plan going into 202627 - Progress Update Oct 26
findings.headline: HRA underspent by £8m in 2025-26 despite prior request for £40m capitalisation direction
findings.detail: Housing Revenue Account achieved £8m underspend from higher leaseholder charges, lower interest costs, and lower overhead recharges. However, council had previously sought £40m capitalisation direction (borrowing permission) from MHCLG, indicating the underspend is a one-year favourable variance rather than resolution of underlying structural pressures.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand whether housing account pressures have been resolved or merely deferred; the underspend does not eliminate the need for major borrowing support.
findings.figures: £8m underspend 2025-26; £40m capitalisation direction sought from MHCLG
findings.quote: The HRA reported an £8m underspend in 2025-26 This underspend arose from additional income from leaseholder charges, lower interest costs and lower overhead recharges.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Action Plan going into 202627 - Progress Update Oct 26
findings.headline: Council funding EFS repayment through asset disposal programme; £3.5m receipts in 2025-26 with further phases planned
findings.detail: Council is selling capital assets to repay temporary borrowing undertaken as part of EFS. First tranche generated £3.5m in 2025-26. Multiple further disposal phases are planned. This represents drawdown of the council's capital base to address current spending gaps.
findings.matters: Asset sales to fund revenue spending reduce the council's long-term capital capacity and ability to invest in assets; this is a sign of financial stress.
findings.figures: £3.5m asset receipts 2025-26; further disposal phases planned
findings.quote: The Council has implemented the first tranche of asset disposals (approx. £3.5m of receipts received in 2025/26) to finance the temporary borrowing arising from EFS. There are further disposal phases of this plan to support the payback of the EFS.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Action Plan going into 202627 - Progress Update Oct 26
findings.headline: 2026-27 budget set with £20m Exceptional Financial Support; also used 2025-26
findings.detail: EFS is temporary government assistance to manage budget shortfalls while structural reforms are implemented. Council is using £20m for 2026-27 and relied on it in 2025-26. Paper states S151 officer is confident a balanced position can be achieved, but "measures put in place and reviews underway will take time to feed into the underlying financial position" and support remains necessary.
findings.matters: A council that requires repeated year-on-year temporary government support has not solved its underlying deficit; this indicates how far recovery is from completion.
findings.figures: £20m EFS 2026-27; also used 2025-26
findings.quote: In terms of the current year's budget this was set with the application of £20m of Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) which is temporary financial assistance enabling the management of budget shortfalls so that essential services continue to be delivered, while plans are implemented to return to a sustainable balanced budget position.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - Action Plan going into 202627 - Progress Update Oct 26
findings.headline: Q1 2026-27 forecast overspend of £9.3m
findings.detail: Council projects significant overspend in year one but paper notes this is "considerably less than in the previous two years." Management is working to identify and deliver actions to reduce the figure in subsequent quarters, though the overspend shows the council remains in deficit despite mitigation.
findings.matters: A lender needs to know whether the council has a path to budget balance or is in structural deficit.
findings.figures: £9.3m Q1 2026-27 overspend; smaller than previous two years
findings.quote: The Q1 report for 2026-27 forecasts a significant overspend at £9.3m. Work is ongoing to identify and deliver management actions to reduce this figure for the next quarter. Nonetheless it is highlighted that the forecast overspend as it stands is considerably less than in the previous two years.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - updated key risk summary Q2 26-27
findings.headline: Regulatory compliance risk remains high; council noted for no breaches in Q2 but faces significant challenges particularly in housing standards and financial management
findings.detail: While the council reported no breaches of laws or maladministration by the Monitoring Officer in Q2, it continues to face 'significant challenges in complying with an increasing and more rigorous regulatory regime, particularly regarding housing standards and financial management.' The council operates with 'Reasonable Assurance' opinion on overall governance and risk management frameworks, with reputation showing positive trend toward heightened compliance and proactive auditing under Corporate Leadership Team leadership.
findings.matters: A council under heightened regulatory scrutiny carries reputational and operational risk. Enforcement action, intervention, or regulatory penalties could add costs and constrain management's ability to prioritise debt service.
findings.figures: 18 directorate-level regulatory compliance risks; average risk score 10.5
findings.quote: the council continues to face significant challenges in complying with an increasing and more rigorous regulatory regime, particularly regarding housing standards and financial management.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - updated key risk summary Q2 26-27
findings.headline: Business continuity compliance did not reach 100% by end of prior financial year and risk of non-completion is growing due to lack of engagement and staff turnover
findings.detail: Business continuity compliance fell short of full implementation despite ongoing reviews. Management notes that conflicting priorities and ongoing restructures are affecting progress. The council acknowledges that the risk of non-completion is 'growing due to lack of engagement, lack of actions and staff turnover,' and plans mandatory awareness training for all staff. This is material because business continuity failures during financial stress can create secondary operational crises.
findings.matters: A council managing significant financial distress and restructuring needs robust business continuity arrangements to protect critical services and operations. Poor completion signals that governance and operational preparedness may be stretched.
findings.figures: BC compliance below 100%; specific completion % not disclosed
findings.quote: Business Continuity compliance did not reach 100% by the end of the financial year...The risk of this not being completed is growing due to lack of engagement, lack of actions and staff turnover.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - updated key risk summary Q2 26-27
findings.headline: Council is progressing workforce restructures and redundancies as part of savings delivery under sustained financial pressures
findings.detail: The council is operating through a significant period of organisational change with services implementing workforce changes and restructures associated with delivering savings. The risk assessment notes recruitment and retention pressures in critical and specialist areas, employee turnover during periods of change, and the need to manage the scale and pace of change while retaining critical skills and organisational knowledge. A new Talent function has been established and recruitment processes are under review to reduce reliance on agency staffing.
findings.matters: Workforce stability and retention of critical skills is essential for a council to deliver services and achieve savings targets. High turnover, recruitment freezes, and restructuring during financial stress increase execution risk on the savings plan the council is relying on to balance its budget.
findings.figures: Not specified in detail; workforce changes are part of an ongoing restructure programme
findings.quote: The Council continues to operate through a significant period of organisational change, with services progressing workforce changes and restructures associated with the delivery of savings.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - updated key risk summary Q2 26-27
findings.headline: Council has commissioned an independent external financial review and updated capital and treasury strategies to reduce external debt
findings.detail: In July 2026, Cabinet formally commissioned an independent external review of financial management, whose findings were not yet available at Q2 reporting. Following a fundamental review of the capital programme, both the Capital Strategy and Treasury Management Strategies have been updated to reflect the need to reduce external debt and its impact on revenue. Exceptional Financial Support is planned to be funded by a programme of asset disposals subject to Cabinet approval.
findings.matters: The decision to reduce external debt and the commissioning of an independent review signal the council recognises structural financial problems. Asset disposals to fund operations—rather than capital investment—indicate constrained liquidity and raising questions about long-term asset base sustainability.
findings.figures: Exceptional Financial Support programme via asset disposals; capital programme and borrowing requirements being actively reduced
findings.quote: Following a fundamental review of the Capital Programme, the Capital Strategy & Treasury Management Strategies have been updated to reflect the need to reduce external debt and the impact on revenue.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - updated key risk summary Q2 26-27
findings.headline: Building Safety Act, Decent Homes Standard and net-zero targets are increasing housing expenditure without matching funding
findings.detail: The council's HRA is structurally underfunded due to government-imposed rent caps and limits on rent increases. New statutory requirements under the Building Safety Act, Decent Homes Standard, and net-zero targets drive costs without corresponding funding. The council has a Lambeth Disrepair Case Reduction Action Plan 2025-27, Awaab's Law readiness group with eight workstreams, and a resident-led damp task and finish group, but faces significant ongoing regulatory compliance challenges particularly around housing standards.
findings.matters: These are structural cost drivers that will constrain the council's ability to balance revenue budgets. A lender needs to see how the council is managing these unavoidable cost pressures and whether they are affecting the overall financial position.
findings.figures: 18 directorate-level regulatory compliance risks identified, averaging score 10.5 (medium/amber category)
findings.quote: New requirements under Building Safety Act, Decent Homes Standard, and net-zero targets increase expenditure without matching funding

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - updated key risk summary Q2 26-27
findings.headline: Financial risk remains rated High despite monthly monitoring, quarterly reporting and spend control panels in place
findings.detail: The council is in underfunded position with inadequate reserves and sustained cost pressures across services including homelessness, social care, and inflation. Despite monthly monitoring, quarterly reporting to Cabinet, spend control panels, and a budget accountability framework, the financial risk remains rated High (32). An independent external financial review was commissioned in July 2026, and cross-party Budget Working Group has begun reviewing budget proposals for a four-year Medium-Term Financial Strategy.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the council's ability to service debt and maintain financial stability. A council in 'critically adverse financial position' with high-level, sustained, structural pressures signals material repayment risk.
findings.figures: Risk rating: inherent High (32), current High (32), target Medium (12); risk appetite level 8
findings.quote: The Council faces a critically adverse financial position, with underfunding, inadequate reserves, and sustained cost pressures across key Lambeth 2030 Ambitions and service areas.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - IA Progress Update October 2026
findings.headline: Audit recommendation implementation rates have declined to 57% for high priority and 58% for medium priority, against an 85% target; 20 high priority and 45 medium priority actions are overdue.
findings.detail: The council's implementation of agreed audit recommendations has declined compared to previous reporting periods. Implementation rates for high priority actions stand at 57% (target 85%) and medium priority at 58%. Of open actions, 20% of high priority and 42% of medium priority actions have exceeded their target implementation date. The paper flags this as declining and 'materially below target', noting that the overdue actions concern 'may delay the mitigation of known control weaknesses and increase exposure to governance, financial and operational risks'.
findings.matters: Slow implementation of audit findings leaves known control weaknesses unaddressed longer, extending the period during which the council is exposed to financial, governance and operational risks.
findings.figures: Open high priority actions: 99 total (57% implemented, 20 overdue). Open medium priority actions: 106 total (58% implemented, 45 overdue). Target: 85% for both.
findings.quote: The volume of overdue high-priority actions remains a concern as it may delay the mitigation of known control weaknesses and increase exposure to governance, financial and operational risks.

findings.paper_title: Appendix A - IA Progress Update October 2026
findings.headline: Limited assurance issued for Children's Direct Payments and Purchase Cards; emerging weaknesses identified in Purchase Order compliance.
findings.detail: Two council directorate audits finalised with limited assurance outcomes. Children's Direct Payments audit identified weaknesses in ongoing monitoring, reconciliation, refund arrangements, and retention of signed user agreements. Purchase Cards audit found gaps in policy compliance, insufficient evidence of approved spending limit enhancements, significant backlog of unapproved transactions, and inconsistent monitoring. Draft reports indicate Purchase Orders will receive split opinion with limited assurance for the orders element and Parking likely limited assurance. The paper describes these as 'recurring issues in the consistent application of established financial controls'.
findings.matters: Recurring control weaknesses in spending, direct payments and procurement suggest systemic compliance problems that could affect the council's ability to manage public funds effectively.
findings.figures: Children's Direct Payments: 1 high-priority finding, 2 medium-priority findings. Purchase Cards: 6 high-priority findings, 1 medium-priority finding.
findings.quote: Limited Assurance outcomes for Children's Direct Payments and Purchase Cards, together with emerging weaknesses in Purchase Order compliance, indicate recurring issues in the consistent application of established financial controls.

findings.paper_title: Appx B - Action Monitoring Log 2026-27 - Copy
findings.headline: Maintained schools and nurseries requiring council action group to manage financial deficits
findings.detail: The committee sought detailed information on an action group supporting maintained schools and nurseries that manage financial deficits, and sought clarification on governance arrangements. The council provided a briefing note to committee members in April 2026 and the action was closed.
findings.matters: School deficits can become council liabilities and indicate service demand pressures affecting council finances.
findings.figures: none given
findings.quote: The Committee requested a more detailed response on the action group that were supporting maintained schools and nurseries, including its impact. The Assistant Director agreed to discuss this with the Corporate Director of Children, Families and Education and provide further information on governance and managing financial deficits.

findings.paper_title: Appx B - Action Monitoring Log 2026-27 - Copy
findings.headline: Statement of Accounts audit objections from leaseholders undergoing external audit investigation
findings.detail: Lambeth has leaseholder objections to its Statement of Accounts that are being formally investigated by external auditor Forviz Mazars. The council has responded to initial information requests and is actively working through subsequent clarification questions from the auditor. The external audit objection process will determine whether the accounts receive a qualified opinion.
findings.matters: External audit qualifications or objections to accounts significantly affect a council's creditworthiness and borrowing terms.
findings.figures: none given
findings.quote: This action remains open pending the conclusion of external audit's work on the related objections to the statement of accounts. An objection to the accounts is required to follow a formal process which is led by Forviz Mazars in their role as the Council's external auditor. The Council has responded to Mazars with regards to the information that was referenced as outstanding at Corporate Committee last month (March 2026). This response has led to subsequent follow up clarifications which the Council is actively engaging with Mazars on to resolve.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecast £2.5m surplus from reduced borrowing costs and void losses; HRA more stable than General Fund
findings.detail: The HRA is forecast to achieve a £2.544m surplus in 2026-27, driven by lower PWLB interest rates on refinanced debt and reduced void losses. This represents the HRA is operationally performing better than the General Fund and managing its tenant base effectively.
findings.matters: Provides offsetting positive news; shows HRA management is functioning; however, improvement is due to external interest rate environment rather than operational change, so may not persist.
findings.figures: £2.544m HRA surplus forecast; includes £18m of £27m disrepair provision
findings.quote: The HRA is currently forecast to achieve £2.544m surplus for 2026/27. The forecast includes £18m of the £27m provision to account for the ongoing financial pressures associated with resolving the historic housing disrepair claims.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection 0.8% below profile at Q1 with £1.8m billing delays; resident affordability pressures evident
findings.detail: Council Tax collection at end Q1 was £581k below profile. The council notes 'broader economic and affordability pressures affecting taxpayers' ability to maintain payments' with increased direct debit failures and cancelled payment arrangements. Valuation Office delays in banding 875 new properties has also caused an estimated £1.8m in billing delays.
findings.matters: Council Tax is the council's most reliable and stable funding source. Collection below profile combined with stated affordability pressures suggests this will persist; £1.8m billing delay means income recognition is also delayed.
findings.figures: £581k shortfall at Q1; £1.8m estimated unbilled from property banding delays
findings.quote: This all tends to indicate a broader economic and affordability pressures affecting taxpayers' ability to maintain payments. In addition, the Valuation Office delays in banding new Council Tax properties (875) is delaying billing, this is estimated at £1.8m unbilled based on band D.

findings.headline: General Fund earmarked reserves remain low despite EFS top-up; stated to offer little financial resilience
findings.detail: Although the General Fund Balance is now at the S151 officer's recommended minimum (10% of net revenue expenditure) following EFS, earmarked revenue reserve levels are explicitly described as 'low and offer little financial resilience in the context of the challenges ahead.' This leaves the council with minimal buffer for unexpected costs or demand spikes.
findings.matters: Low reserves mean the council cannot absorb unexpected pressures or revenue shortfalls. The council is one significant adverse event away from requiring further government support.
findings.figures: General Fund Balance at ~10% of expenditure (minimum recommended); earmarked reserves characterised as 'low'
findings.quote: Although, following the approval of EFS, General Fund Balance is now around the level recommended by the S151 officer (10% of net revenue expenditure), earmarked revenue reserve levels remain low and offer little financial resilience in the context of the challenges ahead.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation savings of £5.5m not being achieved in 2026-27; implementation delays pushing full impact to 2027-28
findings.detail: Housing Services (General Fund) is forecasting a £5.6m overspend, driven by Temporary Accommodation. Planned savings through long leases (£1.5m), nightly paid reductions (£4.8m before offsets), and incentive schemes (£3m) are not being implemented on schedule. The council now expects full year savings only in 2027-28.
findings.matters: Temporary Accommodation is the council's highest-cost service and primary savings target. Implementation delays indicate the transformation programme cannot execute its core financial plans on time.
findings.figures: £5.576m Housing Services overspend; £1.5m long lease, £1.5m transfer, £1m housing company savings all delayed
findings.quote: Due to the delay to date in their implementation, the total 2026/27 saving is unlikely to be fully achieved, however it is expected that the full year impact will be delivered in 2027-28.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant cumulative deficit reaching £11.2m by March 2027; High Needs Block overspend driven by EHCP commitments
findings.detail: The DSG is forecast to end 2026-27 with a £11.225m cumulative deficit due to High Needs Block overspends. Increases in EHCP commitments and associated top-up costs continue to exceed funding. The council remains reliant on DSG statutory override arrangements, which hold deficits separately but are not a sustainable solution.
findings.matters: SEND pressures are not being managed within budget, indicating demand-led costs are growing faster than funding. This is a recurring structural deficit in an area of rising national demand.
findings.figures: £11.225m net DSG deficit forecast at 31 March 2027; £13.4m in-year overspend
findings.quote: This would leave a net DSG deficit position at 31st March 2027 of £11.225m.

findings.headline: Growth & Environment £8.6m overspend driven by £10m income shortfalls across multiple sources
findings.detail: Growth & Environment is forecasting an £8.6m overspend driven primarily by income not materializing, including Parks Events (£1.2m from cancelled events), Markets (£0.6m), CCTV (£0.4m), and Sports Facilities (£0.4m). The directorate is also carrying £2.9m staffing savings with only £1.4m forecast in-year. Management action to identify mitigation of £9.9m is still being developed.
findings.matters: Multiple planned income sources failing to materialise shows the budget is built on unrealistic income assumptions; £10m shortfall in one directorate suggests income risks are council-wide.
findings.figures: £8.603m directorate variance; £10.077m income variance; £2.928m staffing savings with only £1.4m forecast
findings.quote: Growth & Environment is forecasting an adverse variance of £8.603m at Period 3, representing a deterioration of £0.720m compared with month 2.

findings.headline: Parking income £6.2m shortfall (£6.7m target achieving only £0.5m) due to paused schemes and reduced compliance
findings.detail: The council's single largest income-related saving—parking revenue—is tracking at only £0.5m against a £6.7m target, representing a £6.2m shortfall. The shortfall is driven by paused schemes, increased compliance (fewer transactions), and reduced PaybyPhone usage. Parking was central to the 2026-27 income strategy.
findings.matters: A £6.2m shortfall in a planned income source demonstrates the council's projections are unrealistic and the income strategy is unraveling; parking was assumed to be deliverable without major operational change.
findings.figures: £6.712m target; £0.5m forecast; £6.212m gap
findings.quote: Income targets not being forecasted due to paused schemes, increased compliance and a reduction in PaybyPhone transactions.

findings.headline: General Fund forecasting £9.3m overspend with management action planned but not yet fully delivering
findings.detail: The council is forecasting a £9.303m General Fund overspend for 2026-27. While this has improved by £1.676m from month 2, indicating management action is being taken, significant mitigation actions are still being developed and not fully quantified. The council remains unable to balance its budget from core operations.
findings.matters: Even after receiving emergency government support, the council cannot balance its budget from operations, indicating structural financial imbalance rather than temporary pressures.
findings.figures: £9.303m forecast overspend; £1.676m favourable movement from month 2
findings.quote: The General Fund forecast overspend is £9.303m, a favourable movement of £1.676m from the month 2 position.

findings.headline: Council received £116m Exceptional Financial Support from government and is under MHCLG scrutiny with mandatory independent review and asset disposal requirements
findings.detail: In February 2026, the council's application for £116m EFS was approved, indicating the council was unable to balance its budget without emergency government support. The council is now under increased scrutiny from MHCLG including an independent CIPFA review, with quarterly reporting requirements. MHCLG has explicitly stated its expectation that the council should dispose of assets to generate capital receipts to repay EFS.
findings.matters: EFS dependency is a clear indicator of insolvency; the council cannot function without government support. Any lender must understand this is a government-dependent entity operating under formal conditions and scrutiny.
findings.figures: £116m EFS (General Fund), £40m EFS (HRA); annual borrowing costs £7.4m rising to £8.4m from EFS funding
findings.quote: It is emphasised that as an EFS council, we will be under increased scrutiny from MHCLG as part of this an independent third-party review is currently being undertaken by CIPFA. Furthermore, we expect quarterly meetings with MHCLG to report on our progress in returning to a financially sustainable position.

findings.headline: Council is reviewing the capital programme to reduce future borrowing and its revenue cost
findings.detail: A capital investment review is underway "to minimise future borrowing and associated revenue costs", signalling management focus on debt reduction.
findings.matters: Active management of the capital programme to constrain borrowing indicates awareness of debt sustainability and future revenue pressure from loan repayment.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: To note the latest position on the review of the Capital Investment Programme to minimise future borrowing and associated revenue costs.

findings.headline: Finance directorate is delaying staffing savings delivery
findings.detail: Within Resources, the main overspend is in Finance itself and is "related to delays in delivering staffing savings", indicating internal efficiency targets are not on track.
findings.matters: Slippage in planned staffing reductions within the finance function itself suggests implementation challenges and reduces the credibility of savings delivery.
findings.figures: Not quantified
findings.quote: The main overspend within Resources is attributed to Finance with the overspend related to delays in delivering staffing savings.

findings.headline: Council is using £3.903m of flexible capital receipts to fund revenue spending
findings.detail: The council intends to use flexible capital receipts to support "development and implementation of budget proposals" to a value of £3.903m, a one-off resource applied to recurring costs.
findings.matters: Using capital receipts for revenue spending signals tight finances and depletes resources available for capital investment, a red flag in budget sustainability.
findings.quote: To note the use of flexible use of capital receipts to support the development and implementation of budget proposals up to a value of £3.903m.

findings.headline: Children's social care overspend is driven by placements and SEN transport, reflecting demand pressure
findings.detail: The pressure within Children, Families and Education is "largely from placements and SEN transport", indicating demand-driven cost increases.
findings.matters: Growing demand for high-cost social care placements and specialist transport is a structural budget pressure that does not typically recede and requires sustained mitigation.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this summary
findings.quote: The pressure within Children, Families and Education is largely from placements and SEN transport.

findings.headline: Temporary accommodation saving proposals are delayed until 2027-28, deferring cost reductions by a year
findings.detail: The council's temporary accommodation overspend "is from a delay in progressing the activities related to new saving proposals but are expected to be achieved fully in 2027-28", pushing planned savings into the next financial year.
findings.matters: Deferred savings reduce current-year mitigation options and signal implementation challenges in a high-cost service area that has historically been difficult to control.
findings.figures: Not specified
findings.quote: In Temporary Accommodation (TA), the projected overspend is from a delay in progressing the activities related to new saving proposals but are expected to be achieved fully in 2027-28.

findings.headline: Growth and Environment overspend is driven by income shortfalls, not controllable spending
findings.detail: The council reports that pressure in Growth and Environment is "mainly driven by a shortfall against income targets", making this a revenue risk rather than a cost control issue.
findings.matters: Income shortfalls are less controllable than spending cuts and indicate demand or collection problems that may persist, affecting budget sustainability.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this summary
findings.quote: The pressure within Growth and Environment is mainly driven by a shortfall against income targets.

findings.headline: Lambeth is forecasting a £9.303m General Fund overspend at Q1, though improving from month 2
findings.detail: The council projects a £9.303m overspend at end of June 2026, representing a £1.676m improvement from month 2 but still described by management as "a significant challenge" that requires continued cost control. The paper notes progress on temporary accommodation and social care but signals that further action is needed across directorates.
findings.matters: An overspend of this scale three months into the year indicates the council will spend significantly beyond budget unless mitigation accelerates, requiring either reserve drawdown or service reduction.
findings.figures: £9.303m overspend, £1.676m improvement from month 2
findings.quote: The Council is projecting a £ 9.303m overspend at the end of June 2026, a fav ourable movement of £1.676m from month two.

findings.headline: Business Rates collection at 31.18% against 30.57% target, exceeding quarterly profile
findings.detail: Business rates collection is performing above the quarterly profile at Q1. Collection has achieved 31.18% of the annual 96.20% target, representing a variance of +0.61% above profile. The paper notes collection has held up despite revaluation and changes to reliefs which had been expected to have a more significant impact on collection.
findings.matters: Business rates are less volatile than council tax and more resilient to affordability pressures; collection holding above profile despite operational changes is a positive signal for council income stability
findings.figures: 31.18% collected vs 30.57% target (+0.61% ahead); annual target 96.20%; Net Collectible Debit £203.78m
findings.quote: Collection achieved this month is 31.18% a variance of +0.61% on profile.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care forecasts breakeven for 2026/27 despite underlying demand pressures
findings.detail: The Integrated Health & Adult Social Care directorate is forecasting a broadly balanced position at Q1, with a marginal underspend of £75k. This reflects continued management action alongside utilization of growth funding to support underlying demand for adult social care services. The paper notes this builds on improvements delivered during 2025/26, focusing on stabilising expenditure and strengthening financial control.
findings.matters: Adult social care is typically the council's fastest-growing and most costly service; achieving balance here despite demand pressures and complexity in care packages demonstrates successful operational and financial management contrasting with pressures elsewhere
findings.figures: £0.075m favourable variance (breakeven); underspend across ASC, Public Health and Integrated Commissioning
findings.quote: The Integrated Health and Adult Social Care directorate is currently forecasting a broadly balanced position at Q1 and remains largely unchanged from the M2 position previously presented.

findings.headline: SEN Transport costs forecast £1m overspend, driven by 13 additional pupils and increased complexity
findings.detail: Within Education & Learning, SEN Transport is forecasting a £1m overspend (increase of £0.7m from last month). The Routewise system shows 10 additional routes and 13 additional pupils compared to March, alongside pressures from a proposed London Hire contract extension. SEN Management is separately forecasting a £449k overspend due to increased demand and complexity requiring additional staffing and non-staff costs.
findings.matters: SEN transport is a statutory, demand-led cost that councils cannot easily control or budget for; increasing pupil numbers and costs suggest growing identified special needs in the borough and potential for further uncontrolled growth
findings.figures: £1m SEN Transport overspend (0.7m increase from previous month); 10 additional routes; 13 additional pupils; £449k SEN Management overspend
findings.quote: A snapshot from the Routewise system compared to March shows 10 more routes/ 13 more pupils, in addition to pressures arising from the proposed London Hire contract extension

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account forecasts £2.544m surplus for 2026/27
findings.detail: The HRA is showing a forecast underspend of £2.5m at Q1, mainly as a result of reduced interest on borrowing and reduced void loss. This improves the budgeted breakeven position. The forecast includes £18m of the £27m provision for historic housing disrepair claims and reflects continued implementation of the HRA financial recovery plan.
findings.matters: The HRA is one of the council's largest financial operations; this surplus demonstrates that a major service area is improving financially while the General Fund remains under pressure, suggesting targeted improvements in some areas and different financial pressures across the council
findings.figures: £2.544m surplus forecast; reduced interest on borrowing and void loss; £18m disrepair provision included
findings.quote: The HRA is showing a forecast underspend of £2.5m at Q1 mainly as a result of reduced interest on borrowing and reduced void loss.

findings.headline: Savings delivery gap of £19.803m identified where £44.494m in-year savings targeted (44.6% at risk)
findings.detail: The Council is targeting £44.494m in savings for 2026/27 but has identified a gap of £19.803m (excluding staff savings tracked separately). Growth & Environment carries the largest gap (£12.672m out of £21.980m target), followed by Resources (£2.343m) and Children's (£2.738m). The paper describes this as a worst-case scenario if no planned mitigations succeed.
findings.matters: If 44% of planned savings are not achieved, the council's budget will overspend significantly beyond the current £9.3m forecast; indicates either unrealistic planning or delivery challenges that could impact financial recovery timeline and require further management action
findings.figures: £19.803m gap out of £44.494m target; Growth & Environment £12.672m gap; Resources £2.343m gap; Children's £2.738m gap
findings.quote: The Month 3 savings gap sits at £19.803m excluding the staff savings which is detailed separately below. This is considered a worst-case scenario if no planned mitigations are successful.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant forecasts cumulative deficit of £11.225m at 31 March 2027
findings.detail: DSG in-year overspend of £13.420m is unchanged from earlier forecasts and driven by the High Needs Block, which is seeing increased EHCP commitments and top-up costs. The cumulative DSG deficit of £11.225m at year-end will be held separately under statutory override arrangements. The paper notes an application for High Needs Stability Grant but indicates the council will not qualify in 2026/27 due to its net surplus position as at 31 March 2026.
findings.matters: Accumulating DSG deficits represent demand-led pressures in SEND provision that councils cannot control; they constitute committed future obligations even though held separately from the General Fund
findings.figures: £13.420m in-year overspend; £11.225m cumulative deficit at 31 March 2027; £2.195m net DSG surplus carried forward from 2025/26
findings.quote: The DSG overall is expected to end 2026/27 with a £11.2m deficit.

findings.headline: Council Tax collection £581k below profile at Q1; Council Tax Support non-payment up 77.68% year-on-year
findings.detail: Q1 collection reached £73.083m against target of £73.665m. The paper identifies reduced remittances across all payment methods, increased direct debit unpaid and increased defaults on payment arrangements. For Council Tax Support recipients, accounts with a balance but no payments increased from 2,366 to 4,204 year-on-year, representing 17% of CTS recipients and approximately £180k in unpaid charges. The paper attributes this to broader economic and affordability pressures.
findings.matters: Council Tax is the most stable council income source; deterioration in collection and sharp increase in CTS non-payment (77.68% rise) signals resident affordability pressures and economic stress in the local population
findings.figures: £581k shortfall; CTS non-payment 4,204 accounts vs 2,366 prior year (77.68% increase); ~£180k value; 17% of CTS recipients
findings.quote: This equates to c.17% CTS recipients having made no payment. The expected value of these missing payments is c£180k.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation overspend of £5.576m forecast; savings implementation delayed to 2027/28
findings.detail: Housing Services forecasts overspend of £5.576m at Month 3, despite £14.5m improvement expected from 2025/26 outturn. The shortfall is due to non-achievement of additional 2026/27 savings now delayed. While £1.3m of savings have been achieved, implementation of further measures has stalled and the Council expects full year impact only in 2027/28.
findings.matters: Temporary Accommodation is one of the fastest-growing and most costly council services; year-long delays in delivering promised savings suggest implementation challenges and potential for escalating costs beyond forecast
findings.figures: £5.576m overspend; £14.5m improvement from 2025/26; £1.3m savings achieved to date; full savings pushed to 2027/28
findings.quote: Due to the delay to date in their implementation, the total 2026/27 saving is unlikely to be fully achieved, however it is expected that the full year impact will be delivered in 2027/28.

findings.headline: Staffing savings of £9m targeted but only £2.792m forecast to deliver in 2026/27
findings.detail: The Council allocated £9m of staffing savings to directorates for quarter 1. Forecast delivery is only £2.792m, leaving a £6.208m gap expected to be delivered in 2027/28. This 69% shortfall reflects implementation timescales and restructuring delays across the organisation.
findings.matters: Staffing is the largest controllable cost for councils; requiring 12+ months to implement most planned savings suggests restructuring challenges that could delay wider financial recovery and impact the Medium Term Financial Strategy
findings.figures: £9m target; £2.792m forecast delivery; £6.208m gap (69% undelivered); includes allocation to five directorates
findings.quote: Initial work has identified £2. 792m of staff savings, with further proposals under development and progressing through internal governance

findings.headline: Parking income shortfall of £6.212m forecast where £6.712m is targeted
findings.detail: Parking represents the largest single savings delivery risk in the Growth & Environment directorate. The paper forecasts income targets will not be achieved due to paused schemes, increased compliance and reduction in PaybyPhone transactions. This 92% shortfall on the parking target is the dominant driver of the directorate's £8.603m overall overspend.
findings.matters: Parking is a major municipal income source; identifying 92% of the target as unachievable suggests either the target was unrealistic or operational issues are significantly impacting revenue collection
findings.figures: £6.212m gap on £6.712m target; parking contributes to £8.603m Growth & Environment variance
findings.quote: Income targets not being forecasted due to paused schemes, increased compliance and a reduction in PaybyPhone transactions.

findings.headline: Council reviewing Capital Investment Programme to minimize future borrowing and associated revenue costs
findings.detail: The paper recommends noting 'the latest position on the review of the Capital Investment Programme to minimise future borrowing and associated revenue costs'. This indicates an active management review of capital priorities with the explicit goal of reducing debt and its revenue implications.
findings.matters: Active management of borrowing and capital spending is material to long-term financial sustainability and debt affordability; forward-looking control of debt burden signals the council is managing future revenue commitments proactively.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this summary
findings.quote: To note the latest position on the review of the Capital Investment Programme to minimise future borrowing and associated revenue costs.

findings.headline: Council plans use of £3.903m Flexible Use of Capital Receipts to support revenue budget proposals
findings.detail: The paper notes the council's plan to use flexible use of capital receipts, a one-off resource, to 'support the development and implementation of budget proposals' up to £3.903m. This represents use of capital funding sources to support revenue spend, reducing financial flexibility.
findings.matters: Use of capital receipts flexibility to support revenue spending is a one-off, non-repeating resource; reliance on this signals tightness in the revenue budget and reduces future capacity to fund capital investment or absorb shocks.
findings.quote: To note the use of flexible use of capital receipts to support the development and implementation of budget proposals up to a value of £3.903m.

findings.headline: Resources directorate (Finance) overspend from delays in delivering staffing savings
findings.detail: The paper identifies that the main overspend within Resources is in Finance, driven by delays in delivering staffing savings. Staffing reductions are typically a core lever for savings delivery in central functions; delays signal execution challenges.
findings.matters: Delays in internal Finance staffing savings may indicate broader implementation capacity issues; for a council facing budget pressure, delays in Finance headcount reduction are material to assessing management's execution capability.
findings.figures: Not quantified separately in this summary
findings.quote: The main overspend within Resources is attributed to Finance with the overspend related to delays in delivering staffing savings.

findings.headline: Temporary Accommodation overspend from delayed new saving proposals, expected to deliver fully in 2027-28
findings.detail: The paper attributes the temporary accommodation overspend to 'a delay in progressing the activities related to new saving proposals' but states these are 'expected to be achieved fully in 2027-28'. This indicates the saving plan has slipped by one year but management has identified the issue and stated a recovery target.
findings.matters: Temporary accommodation is a high-cost, fast-growing demand on councils; delays in saving delivery signal execution risk but stated recovery targets show the council has a plan to remediate in the next financial year.
findings.figures: Not quantified separately in this summary
findings.quote: In Temporary Accommodation (TA), the projected overspend is from a delay in progressing the activities related to new saving proposals but are expected to be achieved fully in 2027-28.

findings.headline: Children, Families and Education overspend largely from placements and SEN transport demand
findings.detail: The paper identifies placements and SEN transport as the main drivers of overspend within Children, Families and Education. These are typically high-unit-cost, demand-led services where volume and complexity drive expenditure rather than management discretion alone.
findings.matters: Persistent pressures in children's placements and SEN transport are a structural challenge across councils; understanding trajectory and cost-per-case signals whether the council has structural service pressures or procurement issues.
findings.figures: Not quantified separately in this summary
findings.quote: The pressure within Children, Families and Education is largely from placements and SEN transport.

findings.headline: Growth and Environment directorate main area of overspend driven by shortfall against income targets
findings.detail: The paper identifies Growth and Environment as the primary driver of the General Fund overspend position, distinct from cost pressures in other directorates. The report specifically states the pressure is 'mainly driven by a shortfall against income targets', indicating that budgeted fee or charge-based income has not materialised.
findings.matters: Income shortfalls are structurally different from spending pressures and indicate potential issues with fee-generating services (planning, building control, parking, trade waste); revenue income volatility is material information for lenders assessing revenue stability.
findings.figures: Not quantified separately in this summary
findings.quote: The pressure within Growth and Environment is mainly driven by a shortfall against income targets.

findings.headline: General Fund projected overspend of £9.303m at end June 2026, down £1.676m from month two forecast
findings.detail: The paper reports a £9.303m General Fund overspend forecast for the end of June 2026 quarter, representing a £1.676m favourable movement from the month two position. The report notes this 'continues the progress we have seen over the last year, particularly in areas such as temporary accommodation and social care' but describes the remaining challenge as 'significant' and requiring continued action from Corporate Directors and Directors.
findings.matters: The quantum and trajectory of overspend forecasts directly signal financial control and management's ability to close budget gaps through the year; improving trends indicate traction but the remaining £9.303m overspend is material.
findings.figures: £9.303m overspend; £1.676m improvement from month two
findings.quote: The Council is projecting a £ 9.303m overspend at the end of June 2026, a fav ourable movement of £1.676m from month two

findings.detail: The Monitoring Officer notes that progress has been made in dealing with breaches of court orders relating to housing disrepair, but states that there is still work to be done. This indicates the council has been subject to court orders on housing conditions and remains in incomplete compliance.
findings.matters: Breach of court orders is a governance failure creating legal and reputational risk, and reflects on the council's execution capability in property maintenance and service delivery
findings.figures: Court order breaches on housing disrepair cases remain outstanding
findings.quote: progress made to deal with breaches of court orders in relation to housing disrepair cases is noted, but there is still work to be done.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Five external audit statutory recommendations from 2024-25 remain in implementation
findings.detail: External auditors issued five statutory recommendations in March 2025 covering the council's financial position, reserves, Medium-Term Financial Strategy, and the financial considerations of bringing Homes for Lambeth in-house. Multiple actions remain ongoing as at the AGS date.
findings.matters: Statutory recommendations that remain in implementation phase indicate significant issues external audit deemed serious enough to require formal intervention
findings.figures: Five statutory recommendations issued March 2025; progress ongoing through 2025-26
findings.quote: The five statutory recommendations were considered and responded to by the Council on 5 March 2025. The recommendations relate to the Council's financial position and cover the financial year 2024-25, the budget for 2025-26 and the Medium-Term Financial Strategy period, the Council's reserves position and the Council's progress on the financial considerations of the decision to bring Homes for Lambeth in house.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Council reserves were substantially depleted and are being restored through asset sales to repay Exceptional Financial Support
findings.detail: Reserves had reduced substantially in recent years as the council responded to financial challenges. Exceptional Financial Support was used to restore reserves to recommended levels. The council has agreed to fund the cost of EFS through asset disposals in line with its Strategic Asset Management Framework.
findings.matters: The council's financial resilience depends on successfully executing asset disposals as planned to repay EFS; any shortfall in sale proceeds or delay in execution would create additional financial pressure
findings.figures: Reserves reduced substantially; EFS used to restore to recommended level
findings.quote: The level of reserves had reduced substantially in recent years as the Council has responded to significant financial challenges arising from service demand pressures and structural underfunding. The application of EFS to restore reserves to the recommended level enabled the Council's financial resilience to be established at an earlier opportunity than would have otherwise been the case. This was agreed on the basis that the cost of the EFS will be funded by asset disposals in line with the Council's agreed Strategic Asset Management Framework.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 Appendix A Final
findings.headline: The council must deliver £46m of savings in 2026-27 to maintain financial stability
findings.detail: The 2026-27 budget approved in March 2026 includes agreed savings of £46m. The Chief Finance Officer identifies delivery of these savings as critical to the council's financial stability and resilience going forward, but execution capability in a challenging operating environment remains unproven.
findings.matters: This is a very substantial savings requirement that the council has identified as critical but has not yet demonstrated delivery capability for, particularly given control weaknesses and demand pressures in the services where savings must come from
findings.figures: £46m of agreed savings required for 2026-27
findings.quote: The delivery of the Budget 2026-27, within its resource envelope, including the agreed savings of £46m, which was approved by Council in March 2026, is critical to the financial stability and resilience of the Council.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Temporary accommodation and social care demand is creating significant General Fund overspends
findings.detail: The council faces sustained demand increases in temporary accommodation and social care that are stretching the availability of properties and placements. These demand-led pressures are the primary driver of the council's General Fund financial difficulties and the need for Exceptional Financial Support.
findings.matters: These are structural service pressures that are not being absorbed by available resources and are the root cause of the council's financial sustainability challenge, with no obvious containment mechanisms
findings.figures: Increasing demand in temporary accommodation and social care driving significant General Fund overspends
findings.quote: These pressures are most evident in high-demand services such as temporary accommodation and social care, where increasing demand is stretching the availability of resources, including properties and placements, and contributing to significant financial pressures within the Council's General Fund.

findings.paper_title: Annual Governance Statement 2025-2026 Appendix A Final
findings.headline: Lambeth is in receipt of Exceptional Financial Support for the General Fund and is implementing a financial sustainability plan
findings.detail: The council has applied for Exceptional Financial Support (EFS) for the General Fund for three consecutive financial years (2024-25, 2025-26, 2026-27) due to severe pressures from demand-led services. It is working on a plan to restore financial sustainability through a significant savings and transformation programme and asset disposals.
findings.matters: EFS indicates central government has assessed the council's financial position as requiring emergency support, signalling severe financial distress beyond normal budget pressures and raising fundamental questions about financial sustainability
findings.figures: Exceptional Financial Support approved for 2024-25, 2025-26, and 2026-27
findings.quote: The council is in receipt of Exceptional Financial Support in relation to the General Fund and is working on the plan to restore financial sustainability through a significant savings and transformation programme and asset disposals.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: Tenancy Management Organisations show consistently weaker control environments, representing heightened governance and oversight risk
findings.detail: TMO audits indicate consistently weaker control environments within these organisations. While these fall outside direct council control, they represent an area of heightened governance and oversight risk. Of three TMOs audited, two received Limited assurance and one received None.
findings.matters: TMOs manage council-owned housing and represent contingent governance risk. Weak controls in these entities can lead to cost overruns, service failures affecting tenants, and reputational damage to the council. Lenders may hold TMO debt or view them as a liability claim.
findings.figures: Three TMOs audited: Cottington Close (Limited); Loughborough Estate Management Board (None); Wellington Mills (Limited)
findings.quote: TMO audits indicate consistently weaker control environments within these organisations. While these fall outside direct council control, they represent an area of heightened governance and oversight risk, reflected in the overall assessment of uneven assurance across the control environment

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: Cyber security controls assessed as limited; core arrangements in place but critical elements of control maturity require strengthening
findings.detail: Cyber security received a Limited assurance rating on both design and operation. Core cyber security arrangements and governance are in place, but important elements of control maturity and assurance require strengthening. The audit notes improvement is needed to embed a more consistent, proactive and regularly reviewed approach to cyber resilience across the Council.
findings.matters: Weak cyber controls create operational and financial risk: service disruption threatens revenue collection, data loss exposure creates reputational and legal liability, and ransomware incidents have bankrupted councils. This is a control environment gap in a council already under financial stress.
findings.figures: Limited assurance on both design and operation of cyber security
findings.quote: Cyber Security Assurance Limited Limited Core cyber security arrangements and governance are in place, but important elements of control maturity and assurance require strengthening. Improvement is needed to embed a more consistent, proactive and regularly reviewed approach to cyber resilience across the Council.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: 16 medium-priority audit actions overdue by up to 461 days, with oversight and governance monitoring ongoing
findings.detail: Of all open high and medium priority actions, 16 medium-priority actions are overdue. Days overdue range from 6 to 461 days. Senior Management and the Audit Committee have maintained oversight, with directors attending assurance meetings to explain delays. Implementation rates improved to 91% for high-priority and 69% for medium-priority actions, up from 54% in 24/25.
findings.matters: Overdue audit remediation over a year old signals either weak governance response or systemic issues too entrenched to fix quickly. The fact that some actions are 461 days overdue indicates sustained control gaps.
findings.figures: 0 high-priority overdue; 16 medium-priority overdue; days overdue range from 6 to 461 days; 91% high-priority implementation rate; 69% medium-priority implementation rate
findings.quote: Of all the open High and Medium priority actions the following are overdue: Children Families & Education 0 (high) / 8 (medium); Growth & Environment 0 (high) / 8 (medium); Housing 0 (high) / 1 (medium); Resources 0 (high) / 7 (medium). Days overdue range from 6 to 461 days.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: Control weaknesses concentrated in demand-led services including homelessness, children's placements and asylum-seeking children
findings.detail: A significant proportion of limited assurance outcomes was identified in high-risk service areas subject to sustained demand pressures and operational complexity. Specific limited assurance findings include homelessness/temporary accommodation, homelessness and private rented sector offers, unaccompanied asylum-seeking children, and children's placements financial processes.
findings.matters: Weak controls in high-cost, unpredictable demand-led services—where spend can spike rapidly—directly threaten financial forecasting and budget control. These are areas where overspends propagate quickly.
findings.figures: Limited assurance ratings on: Homelessness/Temporary Accommodation; Homelessness & Private Rented Sector; Unaccompanied Asylum-Seeking Children; Children's Placements Financial Processes
findings.quote: A significant proportion of limited assurance outcomes has been identified in a number of high-risk service areas, particularly those subject to: sustained demand pressures, operational complexity, and reliance on consistent application of processes and controls.

findings.paper_title: Internal Audit Annual Report and Conclusion 2025-26
findings.headline: Council requires exceptional financial support to maintain financial sustainability
findings.detail: The approved Medium Term Financial Strategy for 2026/27 confirms Lambeth needs exceptional financial support. This reflects underlying pressures including demand-led services and the level of savings and transformation required over the medium term. The audit notes this financial context represents a significant organisational risk.
findings.matters: A council needing exceptional financial support to stay solvent is a primary concern for lenders and signals structural financial stress beyond normal budget pressures.
findings.figures: Medium Term Financial Strategy 2026/27; exceptional financial support confirmed as required
findings.quote: The approved Medium Term Financial Strategy (MTFS) and Budget for 2026/27 confirms that the Council has required exceptional financial support to maintain financial sustainability. This reflects the scale of underlying pressures, including demand-led services and the level of savings and transformation required over the medium term.
